q: A producer wants a longer list of permitted varieties and a wider boundary than his designation of origin allows, and still wants to name a real region on the label. Which European category takes that wine?
opts: A national quality tier standing outside the European system
A registered collective trademark
A protected designation of origin with a derogation
A protected geographical indication
exp: The broader category exists precisely to house good wine that does not fit the local rulebook, and it is where varietal labelling and experimental plantings live across most of Europe. Its zones are typically far larger, sometimes covering a whole river basin or province.

q: A cheap European bottle names no region whatever, yet prints the grape variety and the year on its front label. What is that bottle's standing in European wine law?
opts: A protected geographical indication whose region was omitted by choice
Wine with no geographical indication
An unlawful label, since variety and year may be printed only under a name protected in law
Wine sold under a trademark, which exempts it from origin rules
exp: Before the reform this tier could name neither, which left cheap wine with nothing to say but a brand name. Opening variety and vintage to it created an enormous market in wine sold by grape rather than by place, and the claims are certified even though no region is named.

q: Italy prints DOCG, Spain prints DO and France prints appellation controlee, though all three wines sit in the same European category. What is the standing of those national words?
opts: They are marketing phrases that carried legal weight once and lost it when the European categories arrived
They are protected traditional terms a member state may keep using for wines in the European category
They are transitional wording due to be withdrawn from all labels
They are trademarks owned by each country's producers' association
exp: The reform harmonised the categories without erasing a century of national vocabulary, so both layers are lawful and either may appear. It is the reason a sommelier still has to know four or five sets of initials that all denote the same European object.

q: A name protected in one member state is enforceable in every other without any further application anywhere. What makes that so?
opts: Each member state automatically copies the others' registers into its own
Registration is made once at European level and protects the name across the whole union
The producer must lodge a separate filing in each state, but the fee is waived
Protection follows the wine, so it applies only where the wine is actually sold
exp: A single European register holds every protected wine, food and spirit name, and an entry on it binds every member state at once. Protection is territorial, though, so the same name has to be defended by separate agreement or registration outside the union.

q: Planting a new commercial vineyard in the European Union needs something no Australian or Californian grower has to obtain. What?
opts: Membership of the local co-operative, which holds the planting rights for its whole district
An authorisation from the member state, granted within a capped national total each year
A minimum holding of five hectares of vineyard
The written consent of neighbouring growers
exp: Total planted area may grow only by a small percentage annually, a survival of the older planting-rights regime brought in to stop the wine lakes of the last century. It is the clearest case of wine law regulating the industry itself rather than anything printed on a label.

q: Growers in a southern Rhone village drew up a charter of their own in 1923, fixing boundaries, permitted varieties and a minimum ripeness, and a decree of 1935 built a national system on that template. Which institution was created to run it?
opts: The Direction Generale des Douanes
The Comite Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne
The Institut Pasteur
The Institut National des Appellations d'Origine
exp: The 1935 decree set up a national committee for appellations of origin which took the institute's name a dozen years later and is today the Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualite. Its founding lesson came from the growers themselves: a boundary is worth nothing unless the rules for farming inside it travel with it.

q: Rank the three tiers of French origin law from the freest rules to the tightest.
opts: AOC, IGP, Vin de France
IGP, Vin de France, AOC
Vin de France, IGP, AOC
Vin de France, AOC, IGP
exp: The bottom rung makes no geographical claim beyond the country and leaves grape and method entirely open. Each step up narrows the boundary and lengthens the rulebook, so the freedom a producer gives away is exactly what the name he gains is made of.

q: Who drafts the production rules for a French appellation in the first instance?
opts: The agriculture ministry alone, which drafts each rulebook and sends it out to the growers to apply
The growers' body for that appellation, which submits them to the national institute for approval
The European Commission, which then notifies the member state
The regional chamber of commerce for the department
exp: Appellations are largely self-governing, with the state acting as approver and referee rather than as author. That is why rulebooks differ so much in ambition from one appellation to the next, and why tightening one is a political argument among neighbours long before it is a legal act.

q: Roquefort, Comte and the poultry of Bresse all carry appellations administered by the very institute that runs the wine appellations. What does that reveal about the French model?
opts: Appellation of origin is an agricultural idea
Those foods sit on a separate register that merely shares the institute's name
Only products fermented or matured over time may hold an appellation
Those foods were added to the wine register as an exception in the 1990s
exp: The same reasoning applies wherever a place, a breed or a practice leaves a mark a buyer can rely on, so butter, lentils and olive oil sit on the register beside the wines. Wine supplied the earliest delimitations and by far the most elaborate rulebooks, but the first French appellation of origin of all was granted to a cheese in 1925, a decade before the wine decrees.

q: Vin de pays was the French name for an entire tier until European harmonisation renamed it. What is that tier called now?
opts: Vin de Table Regional
Appellation d'Origine Protegee
Vin de Qualite Superieure
Indication Geographique Protegee
exp: The change was terminological rather than substantive: the same zones, broadly the same rules, a European name in place of a French one. Many producers still print the older wording alongside the new, so a single label can carry both at once and a buyer meets two names for one tier.

q: France once operated a fourth tier for regions working their way toward full appellation status, and abolished it with the 2011 vintage. What was it called?
opts: Vin Delimite de Qualite Superieure
Vin de Table
Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel
Appellation d'Origine Controlee
exp: It sat between the regional tier and full appellation status, and a candidate region had to prove itself there for years before applying to move up. Almost all its members were eventually promoted or absorbed into a regional indication, which left France with the three tiers it has today.

q: A rulebook states its production ceiling in hectolitres per hectare. What is being capped?
opts: The alcoholic strength the finished wine is allowed to reach before bottling
The volume of wine made from a given area
The number of bottles a producer may sell in a year
The total area an estate is allowed to own
exp: The reasoning is that a heavily cropped vine spreads what the site can give across too much fruit, so a ceiling is the bluntest and most universal quality lever in European law. It is set variety by variety and appellation by appellation, and it tightens as the named area narrows.

q: Appellation rules routinely set a floor on the potential alcohol of the juice before any cellar work has begun. What is that floor really measuring?
opts: How much sugar the cellar is allowed to add
How strong the wine will be after fortification
How ripe the fruit was when it was picked
How much acidity the juice is carrying
exp: Sugar in the juice becomes alcohol, so a minimum potential alcohol is a ripeness test written in a unit a laboratory can verify in minutes. In a cold wet season it is the requirement that quietly puts fruit out of reach of the name its vineyard normally carries.

q: Beyond boundary, grape and yield, European rulebooks commonly dictate two further things about the vineyard itself. Which pair?
opts: The make of tractor and the spraying schedule
The size of the picking crew and the wage paid
The rootstock chosen and the orientation of the rows
Planting density and how vines may be pruned
exp: Both are proxies for how hard the vine is made to work: close spacing forces roots down and holds each plant to a modest crop, while a pruning rule caps the number of buds and therefore of bunches. It is how a rulebook reaches into the vineyard without ever tasting anything.

q: Watering the vines is ordinary practice in Australia and California and restricted or forbidden across much of appellation Europe. What is the reasoning behind the restriction?
opts: European aquifers are legally reserved for household use
Irrigation water is thought to carry disease into the vineyard
Irrigation loosens the tie between the season and the size of the crop
Wet soil prevents the roots from taking up minerals
exp: The objection is philosophical as much as agronomic: an appellation claims that the wine reflects its year and its ground, and a tap undermines both. It also lets a grower carry a crop past the yield the rules quietly assume the season will set. Derogations in drought years have become steadily more common, which makes this one of the places European wine law is visibly moving.

q: Officials sample the vineyards through the late summer and then fix the earliest date on which picking may begin. What does that rule exist to prevent?
opts: Pickers being employed outside the declared season
Growers competing with one another to put the first wine of the vintage on sale
Fruit being picked before it is ripe enough
Machine harvesters being used in the cooler part of the day
exp: Sampling gives the decision an evidential basis rather than a calendar one, so the date moves with the season and no fruit is picked below the ripeness the name requires. The rule matters most in cool regions and in years when a grower is tempted to pick early and clear the crop before rain arrives.
